The city hired a night gardener, although it had no gardens.

This was a clerical error. The position had been approved, the salary allocated, and the man had already bought a pair of boots. Dismissing him would have required seven signatures. Giving him a key required only two.

“See what you can do,” they told him.

On his first night, he found a tree growing through the fence behind the bus depot. Someone had tied a plastic bag around one branch. He removed it.

On his second, he watered the basil on the windowsill of the closed municipal café. He had to pour through a gap in the window, using a paper cup.

By the end of the month, he had a route.

There were weeds worth keeping and flowers that needed leaving alone. There was a drain outside the courthouse where a handful of trapped leaves made a small lake whenever it rained. There was an old woman on Bell Street who could no longer carry her lemon tree indoors.

He carried it.

Winter came. With less to water, he repaired the handles of abandoned umbrellas and left them in the library’s umbrella stand. This was not gardening, strictly speaking, but neither was his job, strictly speaking, a job.

In March, the city discovered the error.

“What have you been maintaining?” asked the official sent to interview him.

The gardener thought about the bus depot, the basil, the lemon tree. None of these belonged to the department.

“Things that were having trouble,” he said.

The official looked down at her form. There were boxes for parks, medians, recreational grounds, and other.

She checked other.

That spring, someone planted marigolds around the bus stop. The café reopened. A librarian began keeping a tin of screws beside the umbrella stand, though she couldn’t have said exactly why.

The gardener continued working nights.

Occasionally he found that someone had already done what he had come to do. Those were good nights. He would stand for a moment in his boots, looking at the watered pot or the cleared drain, then move on.
